title: Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Polo makes 2nd landfall on Mexico's Pacific coast

Hurricane Polo made a second landfall on Mexico's northwestern Pacific coast on Tuesday after drenching the southern Baja California peninsula.

Actual Article Body:
Tropical Storm Polo weakened over northwestern Mexico on Tuesday after making a second landfall and drenching the Baja California peninsula, while a strengthening Tropical Storm Rachel churned offshore, threatening more dangerous weather for Mexico's ​Pacific coast.

Polo again came ashore earlier on ​Tuesday near the port city of Guaymas as a Category 1 hurricane after crossing the peninsula the day before, the U.S. National Hurricane ​Center said.

By 2 p.m. MST, Polo's maximum sustained winds ⁠had fallen to 100 km/h, with rapid weakening expected ‌as it pushes farther inland.

Though Polo is fading, forecasters warned its moisture could continue fuelling heavy rain well beyond Mexico.

The NHC said Polo could dump 10 to 15 centimetres of rain across southern and central Sonora state, with isolated maximum totals of 20 centimetres, raising the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Private forecaster AccuWeather said Polo's remnants could trigger a broader deluge across the U.S. Southwest and Plains.

Hurricane Polo threatens Mexico's Pacific coast

Before its second landfall, Polo tore across Baja California Sur as a Category 2 hurricane, flooding crossings, toppling palm trees and utility poles and sending police to block inundated roads.

"At my house we tied all down. ⁠We prepared very well," resident Bertha Lopez said. "We expected it to be stronger, but thank God it wasn't ⁠so disastrous."

Baja California Sur Gov. Víctor Manuel Castro said no deaths had been reported.

Even as Polo weakened, Rachel was intensifying to the ⁠south.

The ⁠NHC said Rachel, about 435 kilometres west-southwest of port Lazaro Cardenas, had strengthened to 110 km/h winds and ​was forecast to ⁠become a hurricane on Tuesday night and a major hurricane by Thursday, moving parallel to, but remaining off the coast of southwestern Mexico.
